They will stay in a small hotel near the field. They are going to train on Tuesday morning. They are going to play the first game on Tuesday afternoon. The second game will be on Wednesday. The third game will be on Friday. The coach will help the players prepare. He will talk to them before each game. The team is going to work hard. They will run fast and play well. After the last game, they will come home on Saturday. The fans are going to wait for them at the station.

question.question: What is the smallest number of wins the team needs to be champions?
options: A) One
B) Two
C) Three
D) All of them

17.description: A1. Month 2. Describing people's appearance and personality with basic adjectives (tall, short, kind, funny). Simple comparatives (bigger, faster). Vocabulary around 475 words. Very short personal descriptions.

examples.passage: My friend is tall and funny. She has long hair. Her dog is bigger than my dog. I am shorter than my friend, but I am faster. My friend is also kind and very smart. She is the smartest person in our class. She is taller than me, and she is taller than her brother too. Her brother is short and quiet. Her sister is the youngest in the family. The sister is small and shy. My friend has long brown hair, and she has dark eyes. I have short black hair and brown eyes. I am thin and small, but I run very fast. I am faster than my friend. I am also faster than her brother. My friend is funnier than me. She tells funny stories, and she makes everyone laugh. Her dog is big and friendly. My dog is smaller, but my dog is older. We are good friends.

question.question: In what way does the speaker surpass their friend?
options: A) They are taller
B) They are funnier
C) Their dog is bigger
D) They are faster

examples.passage: The river is wider than the road. The road is older than the bridge. The bridge is the newest thing in our town. People say the river is the most beautiful. Our town is small but very old. The river is the oldest thing of all. It was here long before the people came. The people built the road many years ago. The road is wide enough for two cars. The bridge is newer than the road. Workers built the bridge ten years ago, so it looks clean and bright. The houses near the river are old and small. The houses near the bridge are bigger and newer. The school is older than the bridge but newer than the road. The shop near the school is the smallest building in town. The market is bigger than the shop. People walk on the bridge every day to go to the market. The river runs under the bridge.

question.question: Which of the following is the youngest in age?
options: A) The river
B) The road
C) The bridge
D) The town

18.description: A1. Month 2. Simple directions and location vocabulary (turn left, go straight, next to the library). Asking and giving basic directions. Vocabulary near 525 words. Commands and imperatives appear.

examples.passage: Go straight and turn left. The school is next to the park. Where is the library? It is on Main Street, after the store. To get to the school from my house, walk straight for two minutes. Turn left at the end of my street. Walk past the bus stop. The school is next to the park, and the park has many trees. To get to the shop, leave the school and turn right. Walk past three houses. The shop is on the corner. To get to the library, do not turn at the shop. Go straight on Main Street. Walk past the small café. Walk past the bank. The library is on Main Street, just after the store. It is a big white building. To get home from the library, walk back the same way. Turn right at the school. Then walk straight, and you are home.

question.question: If you are walking toward the library on Main Street, what do you pass before reaching it?
options: A) The school
B) The park
C) The store
D) A left turn

examples.passage: To find the museum, walk to the river first. Then turn right and follow the path. The museum is between the old church and the bank. Do not cross the bridge. From the train station, leave by the main door. Walk straight ahead to the river. The river is very close. When you reach the river, turn right. Do not turn left. Follow the path along the water. Walk for about ten minutes. You will see an old church on your left. Keep walking past the church. The next building is the museum. The museum is between the church and the bank. The bank is on the other side of the museum. Do not cross the bridge over the river. The bridge goes to a different part of the town. After your visit, you can come back the same way. Or you can take a bus from the bank.

question.question: Which two buildings stand on either side of the museum?
options: A) The bank and the bridge
B) The church and the bank
C) The river and the path
D) The church and the bridge

19.description: A1. Month 2–3. Shopping and money vocabulary. Simple transactional dialogues. Prices, quantities, and requests. Vocabulary around 575 words. Very short functional exchanges.

examples.passage: How much does this cost? It costs five dollars. I would like two apples, please. Here is the money. Thank you very much. I went to the small shop on the corner. The man at the shop said hello to me. I said hello and looked at the food. I asked, How much do these apples cost? The man said, They cost five dollars each. I said, I would like two apples, please. The man put two apples in a bag. I asked, How much is the bread? The man said, The bread is three dollars. I said, I would like one bread, please. He put the bread in the bag. I asked, How much is the milk? The man said, The milk is two dollars. I said, I would like one bottle, please. The total cost was fifteen dollars. I gave him a twenty-dollar bill. He gave me five dollars back. I said, Thank you very much.

question.question: What is the total cost implied if the speaker buys two apples at five dollars each?
options: A) Two dollars
B) Five dollars
C) Seven dollars
D) Ten dollars

examples.passage: The book costs ten dollars. The pen costs three dollars. I have fifteen dollars. I want both items. After I pay, I will still have some money left. I went to the bookshop after school. I wanted to buy a book and a pen. I had fifteen dollars in my bag. I looked at many books. I found one good book about animals. The book costs ten dollars. I picked it up. Then I looked at the pens. I found a nice blue pen. The pen costs three dollars. I picked it up too. I went to the man at the desk. He said, Hello, how can I help you? I said, I would like to buy this book and this pen, please. He said, That will be thirteen dollars. I gave him my fifteen dollars. He gave me two dollars back. I said, Thank you. I left the shop happy.

question.question: How much money will the speaker have left after buying both items?
options: A) One dollar
B) Two dollars
C) Three dollars
D) Five dollars

20.description: A1. Month 3. Weather and seasons vocabulary. Describing current and seasonal weather. Modal 'can' introduced for ability. Vocabulary near 625 words. Short descriptive passages about the natural world.

examples.passage: Today it is sunny and warm. In winter, it is cold and it snows. I can swim in summer. Can you ski? I like spring because the flowers are beautiful. There are four seasons in my country. In spring, the weather is cool and rainy. The trees are green again, and the flowers come out. I like spring because the flowers are beautiful. In summer, the weather is hot and sunny. The days are long, and the nights are short. I can swim in the lake in summer. I can ride my bike too. In autumn, the weather is cool and windy. The leaves turn red and yellow. They fall from the trees. We can pick apples in autumn. In winter, the weather is very cold, and it snows a lot. The days are short and the nights are long. We can ski in the mountains. Can you ski? I cannot ski well, but I can swim well.

question.question: Which season does the speaker most clearly express a positive feeling about, and why?
options: A) Summer, because it is warm
B) Winter, because it snows
C) Spring, because of the flowers
D) Today, because it is sunny

examples.passage: Bears sleep all winter long. They eat a lot of food in autumn. In spring, they wake up and go to the rivers. They can catch fish with their paws. Bears are big animals that live in the forest. They are strong, and they have thick fur. In summer, bears walk in the forest, and they look for food. They eat berries and small plants. They drink water from the rivers and lakes. In autumn, the food is everywhere. The bears eat a lot. They eat fish, nuts, and many berries. They get fat. Then the cold winter comes. The snow falls, and the rivers freeze. The bears go into deep holes. They sleep for many months. They do not eat or drink. In spring, the snow melts. The bears wake up. They are very thin and very hungry. They go to the rivers. They can catch fish with their paws. They eat all day.

question.question: Why do bears probably eat a lot of food in autumn?
options: A) Because rivers have more fish in autumn
B) Because they need food stored for the long winter sleep
C) Because spring food is hard for them to find
D) Because their paws are stronger in autumn

21.description: A1. Month 3. Food and meals — describing what people eat and when. Simple 'would like' for polite requests. Cooking verbs (cook, boil, fry). Vocabulary around 675 words. A simple scene at a table or in a kitchen.

examples.passage: For breakfast I eat eggs and bread. My mother cooks dinner every night. Would you like some soup? Yes, please. I like soup a lot. In our family, we eat three meals a day. For breakfast, I eat eggs and bread, and I drink tea. My father eats only fruit. My sister eats cereal with milk. My mother does not eat much in the morning. For lunch, we usually eat at school or at work. I take a sandwich and an apple in my bag. After school, I sometimes have a small snack at home. My mother cooks dinner every night. She is a very good cook. She often boils vegetables and fries fish. Sometimes she makes soup with rice. Tonight she is making chicken soup. My mother asks me, Would you like some soup? Yes, please. I like soup a lot, especially when it is cold outside. We sit at the table together and talk about our day.

question.question: Who is responsible for preparing the evening meal in this household?
options: A) The speaker alone
B) The speaker's mother
C) Both the speaker and the mother
D) The person being offered soup

examples.passage: Long ago, people did not have stoves. They cooked their food over a fire outside. They boiled water in a heavy pot. Today we have many easy ways to cook, but some people still like to cook over a fire. In old times, every family had a small fire pit near their house. They put wood in the pit and lit it every morning. They hung a large pot over the fire. They boiled water in this heavy pot for soup, for tea, and for washing. They fried meat on a flat hot stone next to the fire. They baked bread in a clay box. Cooking took many hours every day. Today most people use modern stoves. We can boil water in just a few minutes. We can cook a meal very fast. But some people still like to cook over a fire on weekends. They say food cooked over a fire has a special taste that no stove can give.

question.question: What does the passage suggest about cooking over a fire today?
options: A) It is no longer possible to cook over a fire
B) Everyone uses a stove now and not a fire
C) Some people still choose to cook over a fire by preference
D) People cannot boil water in a pot anymore

22.description: A1. Month 3. Hobbies and free-time activities. Frequency adverbs (always, sometimes, never, often). Simple sentences about personal preferences and habits. Vocabulary near 725 words.

examples.passage: I sometimes play football with my friends. My sister always reads books on weekends. I never watch TV in the morning. What do you like to do? Everyone in my family has different free-time activities. I sometimes play football with my friends after school. We meet in the park. I am not a great player, but I have fun. On weekends, I often go for a walk with my dog. My sister always reads books on weekends. She loves stories about animals and far places. She finishes a new book almost every week. My brother often plays games on his computer in the evening. Sometimes he plays with his friends online. My mother often cooks new things on Sundays. She likes to try new foods. My father usually works in the garden. He grows tomatoes and onions. I never watch TV in the morning, but I sometimes watch a film at night. What do you like to do in your free time?

question.question: Which activity is described as something the speaker does without exception?
options: A) Playing football with friends
B) Reading books on weekends
C) Never watching TV in the morning
D) Asking others what they like

examples.passage: Many artists draw every day. Some paint with oil, but others use only pencils. A painter often works alone in a quiet room. The light from a window can change a picture completely. Many artists draw or paint every day. They say that practice is the key to good work. Some artists like to paint with oil because the colors are bright and rich. Others use water paints because they dry quickly. A few artists use only pencils. They say that a simple line can show as much as a full color picture. A painter often works alone in a quiet room. The room usually has a big window. The light from the window can change a picture completely. Morning light is soft and white. Afternoon light is warm and yellow. Some artists work only in the morning because they like the soft light. Other artists like to paint at any time of the day. Most painters keep their work in their own studio.

question.question: What does the passage suggest about how artists work?
options: A) All artists use the same materials in their work
B) Light has no real effect on a painting
C) Artists choose different tools and usually work in solitude
D) Painters always work in groups together

23.description: A1. Month 3–4. Describing a home — rooms, furniture, and layout. There is/are with more detail. Simple relative clauses beginning with 'that' or 'which.' Vocabulary around 775 words.

examples.passage: My house has three rooms. There is a big kitchen and a small garden. The room that I like most is the living room. It has a comfortable sofa. My house is small but very cozy. It has three rooms in total, plus a kitchen and a bathroom. There is a big kitchen with a wooden table that we eat at every day. The kitchen has a window that looks out on the small garden. There is a small garden behind the house, which has only one tree and some flowers. The first bedroom is mine. It has a small bed, a desk that I study at, and a shelf full of books. The second bedroom belongs to my parents. It is bigger than mine and has its own little bathroom. The room that I like most is the living room. It has a comfortable sofa, a soft rug on the floor, and a small table that we put our cups on when we have tea together every evening.

question.question: What makes the speaker's favorite room appealing, according to the passage?
options: A) It has a big kitchen
B) It has a small garden
C) It has a comfortable sofa
D) It is the largest of the three rooms

examples.passage: Bees live in a hive that is full of thousands of small rooms. The bees build the hive themselves, using a soft yellow material that comes from their own bodies. Each room in the hive has six sides, which is a shape that uses very little material and gives the strongest walls. The bees fill most of these rooms with honey, which they make from the sweet liquid they collect from flowers. They also store a yellow powder called pollen in some rooms, which baby bees need to grow strong. The queen bee, who is the largest bee in the whole hive, lays her eggs in special rooms that are bigger than the others. Worker bees feed and clean the eggs every day until the new young bees are ready to fly out.

question.question: What detail in the passage shows that not all rooms in the hive serve the same purpose?
options: A) Each room has six sides
B) The queen lays her eggs in special rooms
C) Bees make honey from flowers
D) The queen is the largest bee in the hive

24.description: A1. Month 4. Talking about health and body — how you feel, simple ailments. Present and past tense mixed in short narrative. Modal 'should' introduced. Vocabulary near 825 words.

examples.passage: Last week I had a bad cold and I was sick for several days. I had a sore throat and I could not eat much. My eyes hurt and my head was hot. Yesterday I had a headache and I felt very tired all day. I went to the doctor in the morning. The doctor checked my throat and listened to my chest. She said that I should sleep more. She also said that I should drink more water and eat fresh fruit. She told me that I should not work for two more days. I came home and rested. I went to bed early and slept for ten hours. Today I feel a little better. My head does not hurt as much, and I can eat normal food again. But I am still tired. I should rest one more day before I go back to school.

question.question: What does the improvement in how the speaker feels today suggest about their illness?
options: A) They have fully recovered already
B) The headache has not changed at all
C) Their condition has partially improved
D) They need to visit the doctor again

examples.passage: The young runner was very fast last year. She trained six days a week and ran in many competitions. She won every race in her city, and she even won an important race in another country. People said she was the best young runner in the region. But this year, she became very sick. She had a fever for many weeks and could not get out of bed. She was sick for two whole months. The doctor said she should not train at all during this time. Now she is better, and she trains again every day. But she is not yet as fast as before. She gets tired more quickly, and her legs hurt after a long run. Her coach says she should be patient and listen to her body. The coach knows the runner will be fast again, but it will take time.

question.question: Why does the coach probably tell the runner to be patient?
options: A) Because she has already returned to her best level
B) Because the body needs time to recover after a long illness
C) Because she needs to win more races very quickly
D) Because she should not train anymore at all

25.description: A1. End of month 4. Short personal narrative about a familiar event combining present, past, and simple future. Vocabulary of about 875 words. Equivalent to a simple picture-book story or the easiest level of graded readers. Sentences have one or two clauses; content is entirely concrete and personal.

examples.passage: My grandmother lives in a small village about two hours from my city. I do not see her often because I am busy with school. Last weekend, I had no homework, so I took the bus to her house. Her house is small but very clean. There are old photos of our family on the walls. She was waiting for me at the door with a big smile. We cooked soup together in her warm kitchen. She showed me how to make her special vegetable soup. While we cooked, we talked about our family. She told me old stories about my mother when she was a child. I felt very happy. After lunch, I helped her in the garden. The bus came at five and I had to leave. Next time, I will bring her flowers and stay for the whole day.

question.question: What does the speaker's plan to bring flowers next time reveal about the visit?
options: A) They forgot to bring something and felt bad about it
B) Their grandmother specifically asked for flowers as a gift
C) The visit was positive enough that they want to do something kind in return
D) Bringing flowers is a tradition in their family always

examples.passage: Long ago, sailors used the stars to find their way at sea. There were no engines and no radios on their wooden ships. They had small maps of the coast, but they did not have maps of the open ocean. At night, sailors went up to the deck and looked up at the sky. They learned to recognize the patterns of stars by heart. They knew which star pointed north and which stars rose at certain times of year. From these stars, they could work out where their ship was going. But the stars were not always visible. If clouds covered the sky for many nights, the sailors had to guess. They used the wind, the waves, and the color of the water as small clues. Even so, a wrong guess could send a ship many miles off course, and sometimes ships were lost at sea for weeks.

question.question: What does the passage suggest about sailing on cloudy nights long ago?
options: A) It was completely safe because sailors had good maps
B) It was easier than sailing on a clear night
C) It carried real risks because sailors could not see the stars
D) Ships always returned to port to wait for clear weather

26.description: A2. Month 4–5. Graded reader level 1. Short paragraphs about familiar everyday topics. Simple past narrative with time connectors (first, then, after that). Vocabulary around 1,000 words. Compound sentences with 'and,' 'but,' 'so,' 'because.'

examples.passage: First, I woke up early at six and had a quick breakfast of bread and tea. I did not eat much because I was not very hungry yet. Then I got dressed and packed my bag. After that, I walked to the bus stop, which is about ten minutes from my house. The morning air was cool and fresh, and I saw a few neighbors on the way. The bus came on time, and I sat by the window. Then I went to work. The office was quiet because some people were already on holiday. I answered emails for two hours, and after that I had a meeting with my team. We finished our main project together. It was a normal day, but I was very happy because it was Friday and I had no plans for the weekend except to relax at home with a good book.

question.question: Why was the speaker happy even though it was described as a normal day?
options: A) They woke up earlier than usual
B) The bus arrived right on time
C) It was the end of the working week
D) Breakfast was especially enjoyable

examples.passage: First, the seed lies under the ground for many days, hidden in the dark soil. The seed needs water and warm earth, but it does not need light yet. Slowly, the seed begins to wake up, and a tiny root grows downward to find more water. Then a small green stem pushes up toward the light. The stem is soft and weak at first, but it grows stronger every day. After that, the first leaves open out to catch the sun. The leaves are like tiny green hands that collect the light and turn it into food for the plant. Day by day, the stem grows taller and more leaves appear. Finally, a flower forms at the top of the stem, but only if the soil is rich enough. In poor soil, the plant grows leaves but never produces a flower at all.

question.question: According to the passage, what determines whether a flower will form?
options: A) The number of days the seed spends under the ground
B) Whether the stem grows straight upward toward the light
C) The quality of the soil the plant is growing in
D) How many leaves the plant manages to open up

27.description: A2. Month 5. Comparing and contrasting using comparatives and superlatives. Describing differences between places, people, and things. Vocabulary near 1,100 words. Two or three sentences with comparative structures.

examples.passage: I moved from the village to the city last year, and life is very different now. The city is noisier than the village, but it has more things to do. There are theaters, museums, and cafés on almost every street. The streets are wider, and the buildings are much taller than in my old village. People walk faster, and they seem busier. My new flat is smaller than my old house, but it is closer to my work. The trains here are faster than the buses I used to take. My new job is more interesting than my old one, and the salary is higher too. I work with a bigger team, and we have more difficult projects. The food is more expensive than at home, but it is also more varied. Last week I tried a new café near the office. This is the best coffee I have ever had.

question.question: What trade-off does the speaker imply about living in the city?
options: A) It is quieter but less interesting
B) It is noisier but offers more to do
C) It has better coffee than the village
D) It is more interesting than their old job

examples.passage: Mountain rivers and rivers in the plains are very different. Mountain rivers are colder than rivers in the plains, often near freezing even in summer, but they are also clearer. You can usually see the stones at the bottom even where the water is deep. Plains rivers are warmer and slower, but they carry more mud, which makes the water darker. The fish in mountain rivers grow more slowly because there is less food in the cold, clear water. Insects and plants are smaller, and the winters are longer. A fish that grows in two years in a warm river may take five or more years to reach the same size in a mountain stream. However, these slow-growing fish are often considered the tastiest of all. Cooks say that the firm meat and clean flavor are better than anything from the warmer waters of the plains.

question.question: What trade-off does the passage suggest about mountain river fish?
options: A) They grow more quickly because the water is colder and clearer
B) Their slower growth in poorer conditions appears to improve their flavor
C) They are less tasty because there is less food in the rivers
D) Plains rivers produce more fish, but mountain rivers produce no fish

28.description: A2. Month 5. Talking about past experiences with 'have you ever.' Present perfect introduced for experience. Vocabulary around 1,200 words. Short personal anecdotes.

examples.passage: Have you ever visited another country? I have been to Spain twice, and both trips changed the way I think about travel. The first time, I went with my parents when I was young. The second time, I went alone last summer to study the language for two months. Spain was very different from home in many ways that I did not expect. The food was delicious and very fresh, with lots of vegetables, fish, and bread. The weather was warm even at night, which was new to me. People ate dinner very late, often after nine in the evening. Many shops closed in the afternoon for a long break. People talked loudly in the streets, and the cafés were always busy. I have also been to France once and to Italy three times, but Spain is the place I want to go back to most.

question.question: What does the speaker's comment that Spain was 'very different from home' most likely refer to?
options: A) Spain is much farther from home than the speaker had originally expected
B) The food, weather, and culture felt unlike what they were used to
C) Spain was very hard to reach and required a long and tiring journey
D) The food in Spain was noticeably worse than the food back at home

examples.passage: Have you ever climbed a mountain? I have climbed two in my life, and the experiences were very different. The first one was easy. It was small, only about a thousand meters high, with a clear path to the top. I climbed it with friends on a warm summer day, and we reached the top in a few hours. We ate lunch at the top and walked down the same afternoon. The second one was much higher and steeper. I trained for three months before I went, but the climb still nearly broke me. The path was difficult, the weather was cold, and the air at the top was thin. I had to stop many times to rest. At one point, I thought about turning back. But I kept going, and I reached the top before sunset. I have never felt so tired and so proud at the same time.

question.question: What does the speaker's mixed feeling about the second climb most clearly reveal?
options: A) The second mountain was easier than the speaker had honestly expected it to be
B) The hardest experience can also produce the strongest sense of accomplishment
C) The speaker regrets climbing both of the mountains and would not climb again
D) Climbing the first mountain was a more meaningful experience than the second

29.description: A2. Month 5–6. Describing routines and habitual actions in the past using 'used to.' Contrasting past and present habits. Vocabulary near 1,300 words. A short descriptive paragraph about change over time.

examples.passage: When I was young, my life was very different from how it is now. I used to play outside every day after school. My friends and I would run in the park, climb the trees, and play football until it got dark. Now I work in an office from nine to five, and I sit at a desk for most of the day. I used to eat a lot of sweets, especially chocolate and cake. My grandmother used to bake every weekend. Now I try to eat healthy food, with more vegetables and fruit. I used to sleep ten hours every night. Now I am happy if I get seven. I used to read comic books for hours. Now I usually read the news on my phone. Some of these changes feel sad, but others feel right for the person I have become.

question.question: What overall change does the passage suggest has occurred in the speaker's life?
options: A) They now enjoy eating sweets even more than they did when they were younger
B) Their lifestyle has become more physically active and centered on the outdoors
C) Their habits have shifted toward a more settled and health-conscious adult life
D) They have come to prefer working outdoors to working in an office environment

examples.passage: A hundred years ago, cities looked very different from the way they look today. Cities used to be much smaller, with only a few main streets and not many houses. People used to walk everywhere because there were no cars, and most things they needed were close to home. Schools, churches, shops, and homes were all in the same small area. Markets used to be the center of every town. People would meet there to buy food, sell their goods, and share news with their neighbors. Now most people drive, and shopping happens in big stores far from where they live. The streets are quieter because few people walk for shopping. Many small markets have closed, and the new big stores are usually outside the city. People often do not know their neighbors as well as they used to.

question.question: What broad change in city life does the passage describe?
options: A) Cities have grown smaller, and walking has become much more common again
B) Daily life has moved away from a compact, walkable center toward a spread-out one
C) Big stores have replaced cars as the main way that people travel within cities
D) Markets remain the center of city life, though people now drive to reach them

30.description: A2. Month 6. Writing simple letters and messages — informal register, greetings, and closings. Giving news and asking about someone's life. Vocabulary around 1,400 words. Friendly, conversational tone.

examples.passage: Dear Maria, how are you? I hope your family is well and that the weather where you live is finally getting warmer. Things here are going well, although I have been very busy. Last week I started a new job at a small company in the center of town. It is hard work, and the days are longer than I am used to. I have to read many new documents every day, and the system is hard to learn. But I like my colleagues a lot. They are kind and patient with me, and they always answer my questions. We have lunch together every day, which makes the long hours easier. My new flat is also good. It is small but bright, and it has a tree right outside the window. Please write back soon and tell me about your studies. Best wishes, Anna.

question.question: What is Anna's overall attitude toward her new job?
options: A) She dislikes it because it is hard work
B) She is neutral and not sure yet
C) She finds it difficult but is positive about the people there
D) She loves it completely with no problems

examples.passage: Hi Sam, thanks for the photos from your trip. They came through this morning, and I have already looked at them about three times. The mountains look beautiful, especially the one in the photo with the sunrise. I cannot believe how clear the sky is up there. The little wooden house where you are staying looks so peaceful too. I am a little jealous, to be honest, especially because I am sitting at my desk on a grey Monday morning. But I am also glad you are finally taking some time off. You deserve it after this year, with all the long hours and the difficult project at work. Please rest, eat well, and walk slowly. Send me any photos you take of the lake. Talk soon, Pat.

question.question: What does Pat's mention of being jealous, alongside the rest of the message, mainly express?
options: A) Pat is genuinely upset that Sam went on the trip without including them
B) Pat is being playful while showing real warmth and support for Sam's break
C) Pat thinks Sam should not have taken time off after such a difficult year
D) Pat is hinting that they expect Sam to send another invitation next time

31.description: A2. Month 6–7. Describing a journey or trip — past tense narrative with places, transport, and impressions. Vocabulary near 1,500 words. A short connected paragraph with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

examples.passage: Last weekend, my friends and I decided to escape the city for a short trip. We traveled to the coast by train, leaving early on Saturday morning to make the most of the day. The journey took two hours, but the time passed quickly because we played cards and looked out at the changing landscape. The mountains slowly gave way to flat green fields, and then we saw the sea for the first time. When we arrived, the sea was beautiful and calm, with hardly any waves. The sky was a soft blue, and a light wind kept the air cool. We walked along the beach for an hour and collected small shells. In the afternoon, we ate fresh fish at a small restaurant near the beach. The food was simple but delicious. We took the last train home, tired but very happy.

question.question: What can be inferred about where they ate dinner?
options: A) It was a large well-known restaurant in town
B) It was close to the water and likely a local place
C) They cooked fish themselves on the beach
D) They ate their meal on the train

examples.passage: Marie Curie was born in Poland in 1867 into a family of teachers. She loved science from a young age, but her path was not easy. She moved to Paris because women could not study at university in her country at that time. The journey to France was hard, and she had very little money. In Paris, she lived in a small cold room and often did not eat enough. She studied for many years and worked harder than most of her classmates. Later she met another scientist, Pierre Curie, and they were married. Together they began to study an unknown substance. There she discovered two new elements, which she named polonium and radium. The work was dangerous, and they did not yet understand how harmful it was. She later won the Nobel Prize twice, in two different fields of science, which no other woman had done.

question.question: Why did Marie Curie leave Poland for Paris?
options: A) She wanted to discover new elements found only in France at that time
B) The university system in Poland was not open to women in her era
C) She had already won her first Nobel Prize and wished to continue her research
D) Polish scientists generally moved to Paris to work together on new discoveries

32.description: A2. Month 7. Giving opinions and making simple arguments. 'I think that,' 'In my opinion,' 'I agree / disagree.' Vocabulary around 1,600 words. Short opinion paragraph on a familiar topic.

examples.passage: I think that learning a language is one of the most important things a person can do today. The world is more connected than ever, and meeting people from different places has become a normal part of life. In my opinion, learning a language helps you understand other people. When you speak someone's language, even just a little, they open up to you in a different way. You also begin to see how they think, because language and thinking are closely connected. I agree that it is hard work. You have to study every day, and you will make many mistakes before you start to feel comfortable. There will be days when you want to give up, especially when grammar feels confusing. But it is also very interesting, and the work brings real rewards. I think every person should try to learn at least one new language in their life.

question.question: According to the speaker, what is the main benefit of learning a language?
options: A) It is an interesting hobby to have
B) It helps you get a better job
C) It helps you understand other people
D) It is not as hard as people think

examples.passage: In my opinion, watching sport is more enjoyable than playing it, although many people would disagree with me. When you play, you only see your own small part of the game. You are too busy with the ball, with your own movements, and with the players right next to you. You almost never see the wider strategy. When you watch, you see the whole picture. You can follow the way the team moves together, the way the captain organizes the players, and the way the other team responds. You see patterns that no single player on the field can see. I agree that playing is good for your body, and I think everyone should play some sport for their health. But watching is better for understanding the game itself. The best players I know all spend many hours watching matches.

question.question: What distinction does the speaker draw between playing and watching sport?
options: A) Playing builds physical health, while watching offers a fuller view of the game
B) Watching sport on television is more exciting than going to a real game
C) Players always understand the game better than the people who watch them
D) Sport should only be enjoyed by playing it, not by sitting and watching it

33.description: A2. Month 7–8. Conditionals type 1 (real and possible). 'If it rains, I will stay home.' Planning around possibilities. Vocabulary near 1,700 words. Short practical paragraphs.

examples.passage: We have been planning this weekend for a long time, but the weather is making it difficult. If the weather is good tomorrow, we will go to the park near the river. We will take sandwiches, fruit, and a blanket, and we will spend the whole afternoon outside. The children want to play football on the open grass, and my sister wants to read her new book under a tree. If the sun is hot, we will buy ice cream from the small van by the entrance. If it rains, we will change all our plans. We will stay inside and watch a film together at home. I will make popcorn and hot chocolate for everyone. If the rain stops in the afternoon, we may go for a short walk in the neighborhood. But honestly, I hope it will be sunny tomorrow. The children have been waiting all week for this trip.

question.question: What does the speaker's hope reveal about their preferred plan?
options: A) They would rather watch a film inside
B) They are equally happy with either plan
C) They prefer going to the park over staying in
D) They do not want to go outside at all

examples.passage: The town is worried about the rain, which has not stopped for several days. The river is already higher than it was last week, and the fields near the water are starting to flood. If the river rises this week, the farmers will lose their crops, including the wheat that was almost ready to be cut. If it rises slowly, they may save some of them by moving the harvest into the higher fields and barns. Many families have already started the hard work of moving what they can. The mayor spoke at a meeting last night. He says that he will help anyone who needs it, and that the town will provide trucks, sandbags, and a place for any family that has to leave a flooded house. But he also warns that the town has very little money this year, so any longer-term help will be limited.

question.question: What does the mayor's combined message most likely mean for farmers?
options: A) They will receive complete and immediate compensation for any losses they suffer
B) Help has been promised, but in practice it may turn out to be quite limited
C) Only the farmers whose crops survive will receive any kind of assistance
D) The mayor will personally repay the farmers from his own private money

34.description: A2. Month 8. Describing a process or how to do something. Sequence markers and imperative instructions. Vocabulary around 1,800 words. A simple how-to or process description.

examples.passage: Cooking pasta is one of the simplest meals, but each step still matters. First, fill a large pot with water and add a little salt. Place the pot on the stove and turn the heat to high. Boil the water completely before you do anything else. Then add the pasta and stir gently with a wooden spoon to stop it sticking. Cook it for ten minutes, but check it from time to time, because some types of pasta cook more quickly. Test one piece by tasting it. It should be soft but still firm in the middle. After that, drain the water in a clean strainer over the sink. Put the pasta back in the pot, and add the sauce. Mix everything together until each piece is covered in sauce. Serve hot, with a little cheese on top if you like.

question.question: At what point in the process is the sauce added?
options: A) Before the water is boiled
B) While the pasta is still cooking
C) After the water has been drained
D) At the same time as the pasta

examples.passage: To make a simple paper boat, first take a square sheet of paper. Make sure the corners are sharp, because every fold has to line up exactly. Fold it in half from top to bottom, and press the fold flat with your thumb. Then fold the top corners inward to form a triangle, leaving a small flap of paper at the bottom of each side. Fold each of these flaps up to lock the triangle in place. Now open the bottom flap, push it into a square, and press the new folds flat. Take the two top points of the square, and fold them upward to form a smaller triangle. Open this triangle and push it into another square. Finally, pull the top two points outward, and the boat will appear.

question.question: Which of the following correctly describes the role of the bottom flap in the process?
options: A) It is folded in first, before the corners are brought to the center
B) It is left untouched throughout the entire folding process
C) It is opened and reshaped only after the corners have been folded inward
D) It forms a triangle as soon as the paper is folded in half

35.description: A2. End of month 9. A connected short paragraph on a familiar topic with past, present, and future tenses, comparatives, simple conditionals, and basic conjunctions. Vocabulary of about 2,000 words. Equivalent to graded reader level 2 or a simple magazine article for learners. Sentences are short to medium length, and the content is concrete with emerging personal opinions.

examples.passage: Last summer I spent two weeks at the coast in a place I had wanted to visit for years. The town was smaller than I expected, with only one main street and a handful of cafés along the harbor, but it was very beautiful. The houses were all painted white with blue doors, and the air smelled of salt and pine trees. I stayed in a small guesthouse run by an older couple who treated me like a member of their family. Every day I swam in the sea before breakfast, and the water was clear enough to see the rocks at the bottom. In the afternoons, I walked along the cliffs or read in the shade of the old fig tree in the garden. Every evening I ate local food at a different restaurant. If I have time next year, I will go back. I think it is one of the best places I have ever visited.

question.question: The speaker says the town was 'smaller than I expected, but it was very beautiful.' What does this reveal about their experience?
options: A) They were disappointed overall because it was too small
B) Their expectation was wrong, but this did not spoil their enjoyment
C) They expected it to be beautiful and it was
D) They would have preferred a larger place

examples.passage: When the first humans began to farm, around ten thousand years ago, their lives changed completely. For tens of thousands of years before that, people had moved from place to place in small groups, hunting wild animals and collecting plants. They no longer had to follow animals across the land for food, because they could now grow what they needed in one place. Villages grew up around the fields, and over time these villages became the first towns. People had to learn new skills, like building permanent houses, storing grain through the winter, and sharing land between many families. Life became more stable, and the population began to grow faster than before. But it was also harder in new ways. People worked longer days than the hunters had, and one bad harvest could mean hunger for everyone in the village.

question.question: What main paradox of early farming does the passage describe?
options: A) Farming gave people more food but caused them to forget how to hunt
B) Stability brought new comforts and new vulnerabilities at the same time
C) Villages grew larger because animals could no longer be followed across land
D) People had to choose between learning to build houses or learning to farm

36.description: B1 entry. Month 9–10. Graded reader level 3 / simple young adult text. Paragraphs with multiple clauses, subordination, and some embedded phrases. Vocabulary near 2,200 words. Moderate descriptive detail; emerging narrative complexity.

examples.passage: The town where I grew up was a quiet place surrounded by fields, far from any larger city. There was a single main street, a small school, an old church, and a market that opened only on Saturdays. Not much happened there, which is why most young people left as soon as they could, usually for jobs or universities in the capital. They wrote home for a year or two, then visited only at holidays, and eventually some did not come back at all. I was different — I always found something to love about its slowness. I liked the way each season felt long enough to be properly known, and the way you could leave a book on a windowsill in the café and find it still there a week later. To my friends in the city, this seemed like an absence of life. To me, it has always seemed like a fuller version of it.

question.question: What distinguishes the speaker from the other young people described in the passage?
options: A) The speaker left town earlier than the others did
B) The speaker found value in the very quality that drove others away
C) The speaker grew up in a noisier part of town
D) The speaker never noticed how quiet the town was

examples.passage: Honeybees do not fly randomly between flowers, although for many years that is exactly what people thought they did. We now know that their movements are governed by a precise system of communication that takes place inside the hive. When a bee finds a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a kind of dance on the wall of the comb. The other bees gather around it and follow the movements closely. The shape and direction of the dance tell the other bees exactly where to go, including how far the food is and which way it lies in relation to the sun. Scientists were surprised when they first realized that an insect could communicate something so complex, and many at first refused to believe the early evidence. Later experiments confirmed it many times over.

question.question: Why was the discovery of the bee dance surprising to scientists?
options: A) Scientists had not expected bees to return to the same hive after finding food
B) The dance is performed too quickly for any human eye to follow correctly
C) Such precise communication was thought to be beyond the abilities of an insect
D) The bees usually preferred to fly randomly rather than to follow each other

37.description: B1 entry. Month 10. Discussing advantages and disadvantages. Balanced paragraphs with concessive clauses ('although,' 'even though,' 'however'). Vocabulary near 2,400 words.

examples.passage: Although living in a large city offers many opportunities, including better jobs and easier access to education, it can also be stressful and expensive. Rents in big cities are often two or three times higher than in smaller towns, and the cost of basic food and transport is rising every year. The pace of daily life can be exhausting, and many people complain that they have no time for friends or family. However, for young people looking for work, especially those who have just finished their studies, the advantages often outweigh the difficulties. Cities offer the kinds of jobs and professional networks that are simply not available in smaller places. Even so, many people eventually prefer a quieter life. By the time they have a family, the noise, the cost, and the pressure of the city begin to feel less like an exciting challenge and more like a daily burden they would rather not carry.

question.question: What does the phrase 'Even so, many people eventually prefer a quieter life' imply about the appeal of cities?
options: A) Cities are always the best place to live long-term
B) The benefits of city life are permanent for most people
C) The advantages of cities may matter less to people over time
D) A quiet life is only for people who cannot find work

examples.passage: Although solar panels can produce clean energy for many decades, they are not without their own environmental cost. They require rare materials, including certain metals that are difficult to mine responsibly. Many of these materials come from a small number of countries, and the working conditions in some of the mines are poor. However, the alternative — continuing to burn fossil fuels — causes far greater long-term harm to the environment, including rising temperatures and serious damage to the air quality in our cities. Compared to that, the problems associated with solar panels are real but manageable. Even so, the search for cleaner ways to produce solar panels remains an urgent task. Engineers and scientists are now working on new designs that use cheaper materials, and on better methods for recycling old panels at the end of their lives.

question.question: What is the writer's central position on solar panels?
options: A) Solar panels should be abandoned because of their reliance on rare materials
B) Solar panels are clearly the best option and need no further improvement at all
C) Solar panels are preferable to fossil fuels but their own problems still need addressing
D) Mining concerns matter more than the long-term effects of using fossil fuels

38.description: B1 entry. Month 10–11. Narrative past tense with more complex sequencing and embedded description. Past perfect introduced ('had left,' 'had forgotten'). Vocabulary around 2,600 words.

examples.passage: We had spent the whole afternoon in the old part of the city, walking through narrow streets and eating in small restaurants we had read about online. The sun had set before we noticed how late it had become, and we hurried back through the evening crowds toward the station, our bags heavier than we remembered them. By the time we arrived at the station, the last train had already left. The platform was empty, and the lights in the small ticket office were off. We had forgotten to check the timetable that morning, and the fact that the trains stopped earlier on Sundays had not even crossed our minds. There was nothing to do but find a hotel and try again in the morning. We walked back into the city, found a small place near a square we had passed earlier, and went to sleep.

question.question: Who or what is ultimately responsible for the travelers' predicament?
options: A) The train company for leaving early
B) The hotel for being too far from the station
C) Their own failure to check the timetable
D) The morning schedule being too inconvenient

examples.passage: He had walked for nearly a month through forest so thick that the sun reached the path only in narrow bars of light. He had thought himself entirely alone in those long days, except for the birds and the small unseen animals that moved beside him in the leaves. When the explorer reached the village, the elders had already gathered to meet him. They were sitting in a careful half-circle in the open ground at the center of the houses, with food and water already prepared. Word of his journey had spread weeks before he had even arrived. They had known of his coming from another village, which had heard from another village still, and so on back across the forest he had crossed. He realized then that the silence of the forest had been a kind of speech, and that he had never truly been alone, only unable to read the language he had been moving inside.

question.question: What realization does the explorer come to at the end of the passage?
options: A) The elders had been planning to attack him for his entire journey
B) The forest had been carrying news of him long before he reached the village
C) The villagers were entirely unprepared for the arrival of any visitor
D) The journey had taken him far longer than he had originally expected

39.description: B1 entry. Month 11. Describing emotions and abstract states with some nuance. Vocabulary for inner life: relieved, frustrated, anxious, content. Vocabulary around 2,800 words. A short introspective paragraph.

examples.passage: She felt anxious about the interview even though she had prepared carefully. For two weeks she had read about the company, practiced answers in front of the mirror, and chosen her clothes with more care than usual. By the morning of the interview, however, none of that preparation seemed to settle her. Part of her was excited at the thought of a new role and a new set of colleagues, but she was also afraid of making a mistake — of saying the wrong thing, of going blank in front of a difficult question. She sat in the waiting room and tried to slow her breathing. She reminded herself that she had done this before, more than once, and that even her worst interviews had not been as bad afterward as they had felt in the moment. The thought did not remove her anxiety, but it gave her something firm to stand on while she waited.

question.question: Why does she remind herself that she has done this before?
options: A) To remember the questions she was asked last time
B) To calm herself by drawing on past experience as proof she can cope
C) To make sure she does not make the same mistake twice
D) Because she is excited and wants to remember that feeling

examples.passage: The painter had been working on the same picture for many weeks, returning to it each morning before the light from the studio window had fully arrived. He had laid down the underpainting carefully, had built up the figures over many sessions, and had spent two whole afternoons mixing the exact green he wanted for the trees in the background. Now, in the late afternoon of what he had hoped would be his last day on the work, he stepped back from the canvas and felt suddenly uncertain. The colors were right, the figures were where he had wanted them, the composition was balanced, and yet something was missing. He could not name what it was, only that he would recognize it the moment it appeared. He set down his brush and walked across the room to make tea, knowing from long experience that the answer would not come if he tried to force it.

question.question: What does the painter's experience most precisely illustrate?
options: A) A failure of skill that the painter is unwilling to admit honestly to himself
B) A form of judgment that recognizes what is missing without being able to define it
C) A loss of interest in the painting that he has been working on for some time
D) A clear technical mistake that the painter knows exactly how to fix

40.description: B1 entry. Month 11–12. Simple reporting and indirect speech ('He said that,' 'She told me'). Summarizing what others said or wrote. Vocabulary near 3,000 words. A short journalistic or informational paragraph.

examples.passage: A new study on city air pollution was presented to the local council yesterday, and its findings were widely reported in the morning papers. The report said that air quality in the city had improved over the last decade, with measurable drops in two of the most harmful pollutants. Experts told the committee that new regulations on traffic, factories, and home heating had made a significant difference, although the changes had been gradual and the effects were not always easy to feel from one year to the next. They added that public transport investment and a wider network of cycle lanes had also played a role. However, they warned that more work was still needed. Some areas near the main highway continued to record dangerous levels of pollution on the busiest days, and the level of certain newer pollutants was rising. The committee promised to consider further measures.

question.question: What is the experts' overall message to the committee?
options: A) Regulations have had no effect and more action is urgently needed
B) Progress has been made but the situation is not yet fully resolved
C) Air quality has improved enough that regulations can now be relaxed
D) The city's air quality is now the best it has ever been

examples.passage: The historian explained that the war had not been started for the reasons most people believed, and that the simple story repeated in textbooks for decades did not match the documents now available to researchers. She told the audience that the more dramatic events of the final months had drawn attention away from quieter but more important developments earlier in the decade. She said that economic pressure on the smaller country, in the form of tariffs, blocked exports, and the loss of access to certain key markets, had made conflict almost inevitable years before the first shot was fired. She added, however, that no single cause could fully explain such a complex event, and that historians who reduced the war to one factor were repeating, in a slightly more sophisticated form, the same kind of mistake the textbooks had made.

question.question: What is the historian's main point about the cause of the war?
options: A) The war could have been entirely avoided if economic pressure had been removed
B) The popular explanation is wrong and one specific cause can replace it directly
C) Long-term pressures mattered more than is often thought, but no single factor explains everything
D) The war was started over economic pressure, and no other factors were involved at all

41.description: B1. Month 12. Simple argumentative writing — a clear position supported by two or three reasons. Discourse markers: 'firstly,' 'secondly,' 'in addition,' 'to conclude.' Vocabulary near 3,200 words.

examples.passage: There are several reasons why people choose to live in cities. Firstly, cities offer better job opportunities. Secondly, there are more cultural and social activities available. In addition, transport links are usually much better than in rural areas.

question.question: Which of the following is NOT given as a reason why people choose to live in cities?
options: A) Better employment prospects
B) Lower cost of living
C) More cultural activities
D) Superior transport connections

examples.passage: There are several reasons why amateur athletes should rest more than they often do. Firstly, muscles repair themselves only during periods of rest, not during training. Secondly, fatigue makes injuries far more likely. To conclude, training without rest is not a sign of dedication; it is a way to slow down one's own progress.

question.question: What is the writer's main argument in this passage?
options: A) Amateur athletes should train as much as possible to make real progress
B) Resting too much is a common cause of injury for many amateur athletes
C) Skipping rest is counterproductive and damages the very progress one seeks
D) Muscle repair happens during exercise, not during periods of rest

42.description: B1. Month 12–13. Describing social issues with basic analysis. Cause and effect language ('as a result,' 'this leads to'). Vocabulary around 3,400 words. A short expository paragraph on a familiar topic.

examples.passage: Many young people leave small towns to study in big cities. As a result, rural communities often struggle to keep their population young and active. This leads to a lack of workers in local industries, which can make the problem worse over time.

question.question: According to the passage, what is the ultimate consequence of young people leaving rural areas?
options: A) Cities become too crowded to absorb new arrivals
B) Rural industries grow stronger without young workers
C) The rural decline deepens as workforce shortages build on each other
D) Small towns build new schools to attract young people back

examples.passage: When a forest is cleared too quickly, the soil loses the roots that hold it in place. As a result, heavy rain washes the topsoil away. This leads to flooding in lower valleys and to a slow loss of the very land that farmers had hoped to gain by clearing the forest in the first place.

question.question: What irony does the passage point out about rapid forest clearing?
options: A) Farmers gain land but only after they have endured many years of flooding first
B) The action taken to gain farmland actually helps to destroy that same land over time
C) Forests grow back more quickly after they have been cleared completely than partially
D) Heavy rain happens more often in valleys that still have many forests near them

43.description: B1. Month 13. Reading and producing simple news-style text. Active and passive voice used naturally. Vocabulary near 3,600 words. A short news paragraph with basic journalistic structure.

examples.passage: A new community center was opened in the town last week. The building was designed by a local architect and funded by the city government. Residents were invited to attend the opening ceremony, which was attended by several hundred people.

question.question: What does the information about the architect and funding source together suggest about the project?
options: A) It was an expensive private development for profit
B) It was a locally rooted project supported by public money
C) The city government designed the building itself directly
D) The architect personally paid for the whole project

examples.passage: A rare bird, not seen in the region for over fifty years, was photographed yesterday by a local farmer. The image was confirmed by experts at the national wildlife institute. Conservation groups have welcomed the news, though they warned that one sighting does not yet mean the species has recovered in the wild.

question.question: How do conservation groups appear to interpret the sighting?
options: A) As clear evidence that the species has fully and permanently recovered
B) As an encouraging but inconclusive signal that needs further confirmation
C) As proof that earlier conservation efforts were unnecessary in the first place
D) As a likely error by the farmer that the institute should not have confirmed

44.description: B1. Month 13–14. Hypothetical situations with type 2 conditional ('If I were,' 'I would'). Discussing wishes and imagined scenarios. Vocabulary around 3,800 words.

examples.passage: If I had more free time, I would travel more and learn to paint. I would probably live somewhere by the sea. But right now I have other priorities, and I think I am happy with that.

question.question: What does the final sentence reveal about the speaker's relationship to their imagined life?
options: A) They are deeply unhappy with their current situation
B) They regret not having pursued those dreams when younger
C) They are at peace with their actual life despite imagining alternatives
D) They plan to change things and pursue their priorities soon

examples.passage: If I were a young scientist starting today, I think I would choose to study the climate. The problems are urgent, and the field needs every careful mind it can find. But I am not young, and the work I have already done is not the kind of thing one simply abandons.

question.question: What is the speaker indicating about their own career through this hypothetical?
options: A) They have already begun the process of switching their field of study to climate science
B) They believe their existing work is wholly unrelated to what truly matters today
C) They acknowledge what they would do if starting over, but accept the constraints of their actual position
D) They regret not choosing climate science when they were a younger person

45.description: B1. Month 14–15. A sustained paragraph on a familiar topic with clear structure, varied sentence length, and some subordinate clauses. Vocabulary of about 4,000 words. Equivalent to a young adult novel or a straightforward news article. Some idiomatic language, clear logical flow, and moderate descriptive detail.

examples.passage: Living abroad for the first time is both exciting and unsettling. You discover things about yourself that you never expected — your habits, your fears, and your need for familiarity. At first everything feels different, from the food to the way people greet each other. But slowly, if you give it time, the feeling shifts. You begin to feel at home in a place that once seemed impossible to understand.

question.question: According to the passage, what is the key condition for eventually feeling at home abroad?
options: A) Learning the local language as quickly as possible
B) Changing your habits to match the local culture
C) Allowing enough time to pass without rushing it
D) Finding familiar food and recognizable greetings

examples.passage: The discovery of penicillin in 1928 was famously accidental. A scientist returned from holiday to find that a mold had grown in one of his dishes and had killed the bacteria around it. Many others might have thrown the dish away. What made the difference was not luck alone but the kind of attention that was prepared to notice what luck had set in front of it.

question.question: What does the writer ultimately credit for the discovery of penicillin?
options: A) Pure luck, since the scientist had no real role in the events that took place
B) The scientist's foreign travel, which had given him enough time to think clearly
C) A trained mind that was ready to recognize what an accident had revealed
D) The mold itself, which had killed the bacteria without any scientific help

46.description: B1. Month 15. Nuanced personal narrative with reflection. Complex sentences with multiple subordinate clauses. Vocabulary near 4,300 words. Emerging personal voice and observation.

examples.passage: Growing up near the water, I never thought of the sea as something special — it was simply there, the way a wall or a road is there. It was only years later, living inland, that I began to understand what I had taken for granted.

question.question: What enabled the speaker to recognize the sea's value?
options: A) Reading about the sea while living inland
B) Returning to the coast as an adult visitor
C) The experience of its absence after moving away
D) Being told by others how special it was

examples.passage: The old librarian knew every book in the building, not by title, but by the quality of the silence each one created in the room when it was being read. Some books left a tense silence, as if their readers were holding their breath. Others left a soft, drifting silence that seemed to settle into the wood of the tables themselves.

question.question: What does the librarian's unusual way of knowing the books most suggest about her relationship to the library?
options: A) She has read every single book in the library and remembers each one in detail
B) She has spent so much time observing readers that the books are known to her through their effects on others
C) She believes that books are best understood by examining their physical bindings closely
D) She is unable to read the books herself and so must judge them only by their covers

47.description: B1. Month 16. Explaining a concept or process to a general audience. Clear exposition with examples. Technical vocabulary is minimal but accurately used. Vocabulary around 4,600 words.

examples.passage: Memory does not work like a recording. Each time we remember something, we reconstruct it slightly differently, influenced by what we have experienced since. This is why two people who witnessed the same event can describe it in completely different ways.

question.question: Why, according to the passage, might two witnesses give different accounts of the same event?
options: A) One of the two witnesses may simply not be telling the full truth
B) They were standing in different places and so saw different parts of the event
C) Each person's later experiences have quietly reshaped how they remember it
D) Memory works like a recording that gradually gets corrupted over time

examples.passage: A coral reef is not a single organism but an enormous community. Each coral animal is tiny, but together they build the limestone structures that house thousands of species of fish, plants, and other creatures. When the water grows too warm, the corals expel the algae that feed them and slowly starve. The reef does not die all at once; it fades, and the community fades with it.

question.question: What does the description of how a reef dies most clearly emphasize?
options: A) The collapse is sudden, beginning and ending in the same single moment of crisis
B) Warm water has no significant effect on the survival of corals over time
C) The death of the reef is gradual and pulls down a much wider system with it
D) Reefs can recover quickly because they are made up of so many different organisms

48.description: B1. Month 16–17. Discussing cultural topics — traditions, customs, and values — with some comparison between cultures. Vocabulary near 4,900 words. A balanced, descriptive paragraph.

examples.passage: In many cultures, sharing a meal is much more than just eating. It is a tradition that brings family members closer together and marks important events. The food itself is often less important than the meaning of eating together.

question.question: What is the passage's central claim about communal meals?
options: A) The quality of the food is what makes a shared meal meaningful
B) Shared meals matter most during formal religious occasions
C) The social meaning of eating together outweighs the food itself
D) Shared meals are mainly important for bonding with strangers

examples.passage: Throughout history, music has often crossed borders more easily than language. A song written in one country can move listeners on the other side of the world without translation. This may be because rhythm and melody speak to feelings that lie beneath the level of words — feelings that all human beings share but that no language ever fully captures.

question.question: Why does the writer suggest music crosses borders more easily than language?
options: A) Because most popular music today happens to be sung in widely understood languages
B) Because melody and rhythm reach a layer of feeling that words cannot fully express
C) Because translation is too difficult and slow to keep pace with international travel
D) Because feelings are felt in different ways by different cultures of the world

49.description: B1–B2 boundary. Month 17. A passage with moderate complexity and fluency, some idiomatic language, and varied sentence structures. Vocabulary around 5,200 words. The writing feels natural and connected rather than constructed.

examples.passage: She had lived in the same apartment for twelve years, and by now it felt less like a home than a habit. Every morning she followed the same route to work, passed the same faces, bought coffee from the same cart. She told herself this was stability. On difficult days, she was not so sure.

question.question: What does the phrase 'felt less like a home than a habit' suggest about her situation?
options: A) Her apartment is uncomfortable and she wants to move out
B) She has confused routine with genuine contentment in her life
C) She values stability and is fully satisfied with how things are
D) Building habits is always a solid foundation for happiness

examples.passage: The painter worked outdoors in all weathers, even when the wind made the canvas shake on the easel. Friends thought he was being foolish; he insisted that a painting made indoors from memory was always thinner than one made in the presence of the thing itself. He was not interested, he said, in the look of a tree, but in the strange resistance the world offered when you tried to set it down.

question.question: What does the painter's stated reason for working outdoors most clearly reveal about his idea of art?
options: A) He believes painting is a form of careful documentation of every visible detail
B) He values direct contact with the subject because he is interested in struggle, not appearance
C) He prefers difficult conditions because they impress his friends and fellow painters
D) He thinks indoor painting is technically inferior because the light there is too steady

50.description: B1. About 18 months of study. Standard news article or short popular nonfiction. Vocabulary of roughly 5,500 words active. Varied sentence structures, clear argumentation, and emerging idioms. The prose is fluent, direct, and efficient — not yet literary, but fully functional for adult reading.

examples.passage: Researchers have long debated whether cities make people happier or more isolated. New data suggests the answer depends heavily on factors like income, age, and access to green space. Those who live near parks and community spaces report significantly higher levels of wellbeing, regardless of how densely populated their neighborhood is.

question.question: What does the finding about parks challenge in the ongoing debate about cities?
options: A) The idea that income has any effect on happiness
B) The assumption that population density alone decides urban wellbeing
C) The claim that cities always and automatically make people happier
D) The view that green space matters more than any community factor

examples.passage: For most of recorded history, mathematicians treated zero with deep suspicion. The very idea of a number representing nothing seemed contradictory, even dangerous to philosophical systems built on the principle that everything that exists must be something. The eventual acceptance of zero, brought to Europe through Indian and Arab scholarship, was not merely a technical advance. It was a quiet revolution in how the West allowed itself to think.

question.question: Why does the writer call the acceptance of zero 'a quiet revolution in how the West allowed itself to think'?
options: A) Because zero proved to be useful in advanced calculations across many areas of mathematics
B) Because accepting zero required the West to permit a concept its philosophy had previously ruled out
C) Because Indian and Arab scholars had already used zero for many centuries before its arrival
D) Because zero made it possible to write much larger numbers than had been written before

51.description: B1–B2. Month 18–20. Slightly richer vocabulary and more sustained argument. A longer paragraph with a clear thesis, evidence, and a concluding observation. Vocabulary near 5,800 words.

examples.passage: The appeal of nostalgia is easy to understand but hard to justify. We tend to remember the past not as it was but as we wished it to be, editing out the discomforts and magnifying the warmth. Politicians who promise to restore a golden age are selling a version of history that never quite existed.

question.question: What is the passage implying about political promises to 'restore a golden age'?
options: A) Such promises work because voters remember the past accurately
B) Politicians understand history better than most ordinary people do
C) These promises exploit a tendency to remember the past as better than it was
D) Nostalgia is a reliable guide to deciding which past policies succeeded

examples.passage: Watching a great chess player is a peculiar experience. The board itself looks unchanged for long stretches; almost nothing happens. Yet to those who can read the position, an entire drama is unfolding — possibilities being weighed, threats being prepared, choices being silently abandoned. The spectacle is one of pure intellect, which is also why so few people can bear to sit through it.

question.question: What does the writer suggest about the appeal of watching chess?
options: A) It is enjoyable because the action on the board is constantly changing in visible ways
B) Most viewers can easily follow the underlying calculations of professional players
C) Its drama is real but invisible, which makes it inaccessible to most spectators
D) Chess is a poor spectator sport because nothing of any importance ever truly occurs

52.description: B1–B2. Month 20. Popular science or nature writing. Accessible explanation of complex ideas with concrete illustrations. Vocabulary around 6,100 words. Clear prose with some figurative language.

examples.passage: The deep ocean is one of the least understood places on Earth. Below a thousand meters, sunlight disappears entirely and the water is near freezing. Yet life thrives there, in forms so unusual they seem to belong to another world — fish with their own built-in lights, creatures that can survive pressures that would crush a submarine.

question.question: The comparison to 'another world' is used to convey what about deep-sea life?
options: A) Deep-sea creatures may have come from outer space originally
B) The ocean floor is as little explored as other planets are
C) The creatures are so strange in form that they go beyond ordinary expectation
D) Scientists find studying the deep ocean more exciting than studying space

examples.passage: The ancient Greeks believed that the gods themselves had set the stars in their fixed positions, and that the small wandering points of light were planets — the word itself means 'wanderer.' For centuries, no one could explain why these few stars moved while the rest stayed still. The answer, when it finally came, would require giving up the comforting picture of an Earth at the center of everything.

question.question: What does the passage suggest the explanation of planetary motion required from human thinkers?
options: A) Better telescopes capable of clearly resolving the small wandering points of light
B) The acceptance of a worldview that displaced humanity from the cosmic center
C) A return to the original Greek belief that the gods had set every star in place
D) The recognition that the planets were not really moving across the sky after all

53.description: B2 approach. Month 21. Personal essay style with observation, reflection, and a small argumentative thread. Vocabulary near 6,400 words. Sentence variety increases; the prose has rhythm.
